idiom_name: projection struct + field mask + copy function (jansson json_object_get for JSON payloads)
implementation_notes: C has no reflection and no serialization in its standard library, so the projection is code: declare a narrow output struct (or an outgoing writer) that contains only the retained fields and copy them across, leaving the dropped fields absent by construction; a dynamic, caller-selected field set is modelled as a bitmask or a table of names checked while writing. What replaces the classic filter object is a plain function - project(const struct user *in, unsigned keep, struct user_dto *out) - plus the mask that parameterises it, so there is no filter class to instantiate. The masked/table-driven form is still justified when one producer must serve several receivers with different, runtime-selected field sets; when the payload is JSON and only some keys must survive, a library such as jansson can rebuild the object with json_object_get/json_object_set, but it does not choose the fields for you.
pitfalls: A mask that admits fields the DTO has no storage for silently truncates the contract: keep mask bits and DTO members in one header so the compiler and the reviewer see both.
snprintf/strncpy truncation without explicit NUL termination turns a filtered string into a buffer over-read at the receiver, and the truncated value is then indistinguishable from a legitimate one.
A struct-copy projection does not deep-copy pointers: a retained char * still points into the source buffer, which may be freed or reused (dangling read at the receiver).
Uninitialised DTO padding travels to the wire if the struct is sent raw with write()/send(): zero it or serialize field by field.
